title: Enforce network restrictions on access tokens
summary: S2 access tokens can now be restricted to an allow-list of IP ranges or AWS PrivateLink endpoints, and you can see where each token was recently used from.
body_markdown:
[Access tokens](https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/access-tokens) on S2 already let you scope *what* a client can do: what basins and streams they have access to, what operations are allowed, and for how long.


Now you can also enforce *where* a token can be used from with[network policies](https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/network-policies) , significantly reducing the blast radius of a token getting into the wrong hands.


You can also now see where each token was recently used from, and whether those requests were accepted or denied, in the dashboard or through the[metrics API](https://s2.dev/docs/api/metrics/account#token-activity) .


## Network policies


By default, an access token works from any network. A[network policy](https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/network-policies) is an allow-list you attach to a token when you issue it. Entries can be:


- **IP ranges** in CIDR notation (IPv4 or IPv6), for requests over the public internet
- **AWS PrivateLink endpoint IDs** , for requests over[private networking](https://s2.dev/docs/platform/private-networking)


For example, this policy allows two public ranges and one VPC endpoint:


```text
{
"public_net"  : {   "cidrs"  : [  "203.0.113.0/24"  ,   "2001:db8:1234::/48"  ] },
"private_net"  : {   "aws"  : {   "vpce_ids"  : [  "vpce-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890"  ] } }
}
```


Requests made with a bound token from anywhere else are rejected, so a token that leaks out of your infrastructure is no longer usable from outside it.


## Try it


*Requires[CLI](https://s2.dev/docs/cli)` s2 >= 0.47` , or use the dashboard under **Access Tokens → Network Policies** .*


Create a policy, then issue a token bound to it:


```text
$   s2   network-policy   create   home   \
--cidr   2600:1700:a412:1260:912c:cbf0:b9ec:c676/128


$   s2   access-token   issue   home-laptop-001   \
--preset   full-access   \
--network-policy   home
```


Or in the dashboard, where you pick the policy when issuing a token:


Your browser does not support the video tag.


Policies are immutable and can be shared by many tokens. A token issued by a restricted token inherits its policy, so a restricted service can't mint itself an unrestricted one.


In this example, the` home` policy allows exactly one address: my laptop's IPv6 address (a` /128` ). So the token only works from there.


Now if I try that token from somewhere else, like a cloud VM:


Your browser does not support the video tag.


Over the API, the same denial is a` 403` :


```text
{
"code"  :   "network_policy_denied"  ,
"message"  :   "Request from 44.213.17.82 is not permitted by the token's network policy"
}
```


## See where each token was used


Every access token now records its most recent uses, whether or not it has a network policy: the source address, whether the request was accepted or denied (and why), and the user agent.


In the dashboard, the **Last seen** column on the access tokens page flags tokens with recent denials, and opens the details for each token:


Your browser does not support the video tag.


The same data is available from the[metrics API](https://s2.dev/docs/api/metrics/account#token-activity) as the` token-activity` metric set, and from the CLI:


```text
$   s2   get-account-metrics   token-activity   home-laptop-001
```


This is handy for checking that a new policy covers all your clients before you roll it out, or for spotting a token being used from somewhere it shouldn't be.


## AWS PrivateLink


If your workloads run in AWS, you can reach your basins over[AWS PrivateLink](https://s2.dev/docs/platform/private-networking) and keep traffic off the public internet. Reads over private networking cost[half](https://s2.dev/pricing) as much as reads over the internet.


We've rewritten the[setup guide](https://s2.dev/docs/platform/private-networking) , including how to send account requests over PrivateLink too. It works well as instructions for your coding agent: point it at the guide and let it set up the endpoint. Combine it with a network policy that only allows your VPC endpoint, and your tokens can't be used from anywhere else.


Network policies and token activity are available today to all S2 accounts. See the[network policies docs](https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/network-policies) to get started.
